claim: Pan-neural ribotagging from fed and 3-hr fasted adult animals identified 802 genes that were increased by more than fourfold in the fasted condition compared to the fed condition.
source: We performed three independent biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and confirmed the enrichment of pan-neural mRNAs in ribotag samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). We examined the genes whose expression was most dramatically altered by fasting: 802 genes were increased by more than fourfold in the fasted condition compared to the fed condition, while 647 were decreased by more than fourfold (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pan-neural ribotagging experiments with three biological replicates, as shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Pan-neural ribotagging from fed and 3-hr fasted adult animals identified 647 genes that were decreased by more than fourfold in the fasted condition compared to the fed condition.
source: We examined the genes whose expression was most dramatically altered by fasting: 802 genes were increased by more than fourfold in the fasted condition compared to the fed condition, while 647 were decreased by more than fourfold (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pan-neural ribotagging experiments, as shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Chemosensory GPCRs were significantly overrepresented among the genes upregulated by fasting (133/802 upregulated genes, p<0.001, Fisher's exact test).
source: Strikingly, chemosensory GPCRs were significantly overrepresented among the upregulated genes (133/802 upregulated genes, p<0.001, Fisher's exact test, compared to ~8.5% overall prevalence in the genome; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) of the ribotagging data showing enrichment of chemosensory GPCRs among upregulated genes.

claim: The AWA olfactory neuron expressed a significantly greater proportional enrichment of upregulated GPCRs than expected if chemoreceptor genes were upregulated uniformly across neuron types (24/133 chemoreceptors).
source: We found that the AWA olfactory neuron expressed a significantly greater proportional enrichment of upregulated GPCRs than expected if chemoreceptors genes were upregulated uniformly across neuron types (24/133 chemoreceptors, Figure 1B, green bars; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell sequencing data showing disproportionate enrichment of upregulated chemoreceptors in AWA, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The str-44 chemoreceptor gene showed very little fluorescence in fed animals but a significant increase specifically in AWA in fasted animals.
source: For the str-44 and srd-28 chemoreceptor genes, we observed very little fluorescence in fed animals, but a significant increase specifically in AWA in fasted animals (Figure 1D; confirmation by co-expression of an AWA marker in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence measurements using CRISPR-generated T2A-mNeonGreen reporters, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The srd-28 chemoreceptor gene showed very little fluorescence in fed animals but a significant increase specifically in AWA in fasted animals.
source: For the str-44 and srd-28 chemoreceptor genes, we observed very little fluorescence in fed animals, but a significant increase specifically in AWA in fasted animals (Figure 1D; confirmation by co-expression of an AWA marker in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence measurements using CRISPR-generated T2A-mNeonGreen reporters, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The odr-10 chemoreceptor reporter was detectable in fed animals and displayed only a small, nonsignificant increase after fasting.
source: As a point of comparison, expression of a mNeonGreen reporter inserted into the well-characterized AWA-specific chemoreceptor odr-10 was detectable in fed animals and displayed only a small, nonsignificant increase after fasting, consistent with the fact that it was only mildly upregulated by fasting in our ribotagging data (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence measurements using CRISPR-generated T2A-mNeonGreen reporters, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ser-7 serotonin receptor expression was not affected by fasting.
source: As a negative control, we generated a reporter for the serotonin receptor ser-7, a GPCR in a different gene family whose expression was not altered in our ribotagging data, and observed that its expression was not affected by fasting.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence measurements using CRISPR-generated T2A-mNeonGreen reporters for ser-7.

claim: Animals exposed to aztreonam-treated bacteria (inedible) showed str-44 expression that was intermediate to well-fed and fasted animals.
source: First, we exposed animals to bacteria treated with aztreonam, which inhibits cell division and renders the bacteria too large to consume. This manipulation led to a level of str-44 expression that was intermediate to well-fed and fasted animals (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals exposed to aztreonam-treated bacteria, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Animals exposed to food on the lid of the plate (inaccessible) showed str-44 expression that was intermediate to well-fed and fasted animals.
source: Therefore, we also used a second approach in which we exposed animals to food that was placed on the lid of the plate, rendering it inaccessible to the animal. As expected, this manipulation also produced a level of str-44 expression that was intermediate to well-fed and fasted animals (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals exposed to inaccessible food, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both food sensory cues and the actual ingestion of food act to suppress olfactory receptor expression in AWA.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that both food sensory cues and the actual ingestion of food act to suppress olfactory receptor expression in AWA (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experiments showing intermediate str-44 expression levels when animals are exposed to inedible bacteria or inaccessible food.

claim: str-44::mNeonGreen reporter expression was increased significantly compared to E. coli OP50 controls when animals were fed Comamonas DA1877.
source: Indeed, the levels of str-44::mNeonGreen reporter expression were increased significantly compared to E. coli OP50 controls when animals were exposed to Comamonas DA1877 or Pseudomonas PA14 (Figure 1F), two species that are naively attractive to C. elegans (Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals fed different bacterial species, as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: str-44::mNeonGreen reporter expression was increased significantly compared to E. coli OP50 controls when animals were fed Pseudomonas PA14.
source: Indeed, the levels of str-44::mNeonGreen reporter expression were increased significantly compared to E. coli OP50 controls when animals were exposed to Comamonas DA1877 or Pseudomonas PA14 (Figure 1F), two species that are naively attractive to C. elegans (Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals fed different bacterial species, as shown in Figure 1F, and cites prior work on bacterial attractiveness.

claim: Comamonas DA1877 is naively attractive to C. elegans.
source: Indeed, the levels of str-44::mNeonGreen reporter expression were increased significantly compared to E. coli OP50 controls when animals were exposed to Comamonas DA1877 or Pseudomonas PA14 (Figure 1F), two species that are naively attractive to C. elegans (Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: Pseudomonas PA14 is naively attractive to C. elegans.
source: Indeed, the levels of str-44::mNeonGreen reporter expression were increased significantly compared to E. coli OP50 controls when animals were exposed to Comamonas DA1877 or Pseudomonas PA14 (Figure 1F), two species that are naively attractive to C. elegans (Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: PA14 odors increased str-44 reporter expression beyond the levels in fasted controls.
source: Relative to fasted controls, PA14 odor increased str-44 reporter expression, whereas DA1877 odor suppressed str-44 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals exposed to bacterial odors on the lid of the plate, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DA1877 odors suppressed str-44 expression compared to fasted controls.
source: Relative to fasted controls, PA14 odor increased str-44 reporter expression, whereas DA1877 odor suppressed str-44 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals exposed to bacterial odors on the lid of the plate, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Animals fasted in the presence of mild osmotic stress (300 mOsm) displayed str-44 expression that was significantly suppressed relative to fasted controls.
source: We found that animals fasted in the presence of this physiological stressor displayed str-44 expression that was significantly suppressed relative to fasted controls (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals fasted under osmotic stress, as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The ser-7::mNeonGreen control reporter was unaffected by mild osmotic stress.
source: However, the ser-7::mNeonGreen control reporter was unaffected by this mild osmotic stressor, indicating that these effects are not due to generic downregulation of GPCRs or diminished expression of mNeonGreen in response to osmotic stress (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of ser-7::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals fasted under osmotic stress, as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The ASH::str-44 strain was significantly repulsed by propyl acetate.
source: However, the ASH::str-44 strain was significantly repulsed by two structurally similar esters, propyl acetate and butyl acetate, suggesting that str-44 chemoreceptor expression in ASH is sufficient to confer detection of these two odors (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data showing repulsion to propyl acetate in ASH::str-44 animals, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ASH::str-44 strain was significantly repulsed by butyl acetate.
source: However, the ASH::str-44 strain was significantly repulsed by two structurally similar esters, propyl acetate and butyl acetate, suggesting that str-44 chemoreceptor expression in ASH is sufficient to confer detection of these two odors (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data showing repulsion to butyl acetate in ASH::str-44 animals, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: str-44 chemoreceptor expression in ASH is sufficient to confer detection of propyl acetate and butyl acetate.
source: However, the ASH::str-44 strain was significantly repulsed by two structurally similar esters, propyl acetate and butyl acetate, suggesting that str-44 chemoreceptor expression in ASH is sufficient to confer detection of these two odors (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from chemotaxis data showing that ectopic expression of str-44 in ASH confers repulsion to these odors.

claim: Wild-type animals were strongly attracted to propyl acetate.
source: Wild-type animals were strongly attracted to both of these odors.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data for wild-type animals, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type animals were strongly attracted to butyl acetate.
source: Wild-type animals were strongly attracted to both of these odors.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data for wild-type animals, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: odr-7 mutants lacking AWA had significantly decreased responses to propyl acetate.
source: However, odr-7 mutants lacking AWA had significantly decreased responses to these odors, indicating that AWA is necessary for navigation to propyl and butyl acetate (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data for odr-7 mutants, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: odr-7 mutants lacking AWA had significantly decreased responses to butyl acetate.
source: However, odr-7 mutants lacking AWA had significantly decreased responses to these odors, indicating that AWA is necessary for navigation to propyl and butyl acetate (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data for odr-7 mutants, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AWA is necessary for navigation to propyl acetate.
source: However, odr-7 mutants lacking AWA had significantly decreased responses to these odors, indicating that AWA is necessary for navigation to propyl and butyl acetate (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from chemotaxis data showing reduced responses in odr-7 mutants lacking AWA.

claim: AWA is necessary for navigation to butyl acetate.
source: However, odr-7 mutants lacking AWA had significantly decreased responses to these odors, indicating that AWA is necessary for navigation to propyl and butyl acetate (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from chemotaxis data showing reduced responses in odr-7 mutants lacking AWA.

claim: Fasted animals exhibited significantly increased AWA calcium responses to propyl acetate compared to well-fed animals.
source: Notably, we found that fasted animals exhibited significantly increased responses to these odors compared to well-fed animals (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AWA calcium imaging data showing increased GCaMP responses in fasted animals, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fasted animals exhibited significantly increased AWA calcium responses to butyl acetate compared to well-fed animals.
source: Notably, we found that fasted animals exhibited significantly increased responses to these odors compared to well-fed animals (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AWA calcium imaging data showing increased GCaMP responses in fasted animals, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At lower odor concentrations, fasted animals were significantly more likely than fed animals to approach the food lawn with butyl acetate.
source: However, at lower odor concentrations, fasted animals were significantly more likely than fed animals to approach the food lawn with butyl acetate (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data showing increased preference for butyl acetate in fasted animals at lower concentrations, as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Well-fed animals overexpressing str-44 in AWA were significantly more likely to approach the butyl acetate food lawn compared to well-fed wild-type animals.
source: Indeed, well-fed animals from this strain were significantly more likely to approach the butyl acetate food lawn compared to well-fed wild-type animals, phenocopying the fasted state (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data showing increased preference for butyl acetate in fed animals overexpressing str-44, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: odr-7 mutants lacking a functional AWA did not display a fasting-induced increase in butyl acetate attraction.
source: odr-7 mutants lacking a functional AWA did not display a fasting-induced increase in butyl acetate attraction, suggesting that AWA is required for this effect (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data for odr-7 mutants, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: AWA is required for the fasting-induced increase in butyl acetate attraction.
source: odr-7 mutants lacking a functional AWA did not display a fasting-induced increase in butyl acetate attraction, suggesting that AWA is required for this effect (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from food choice assay data showing no fasting effect in odr-7 mutants.

claim: str-44;srd-28 double mutants displayed an attenuated behavioral response where their attraction to the butyl acetate lawn was similar in fed and fasted conditions.
source: In addition, str-44;srd-28 double mutants displayed an attenuated behavioral response where their attraction to the butyl acetate lawn was similar in fed and fasted conditions, suggesting that str-44 and/or srd-28 are necessary for normal fasting-induced enhancement of butyl acetate preference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data for str-44;srd-28 double mutants, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: str-44 and/or srd-28 are necessary for normal fasting-induced enhancement of butyl acetate preference.
source: In addition, str-44;srd-28 double mutants displayed an attenuated behavioral response where their attraction to the butyl acetate lawn was similar in fed and fasted conditions, suggesting that str-44 and/or srd-28 are necessary for normal fasting-induced enhancement of butyl acetate preference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from food choice assay data showing attenuated fasting response in str-44;srd-28 double mutants.

claim: Animals fasted undergoing osmotic stress were no more likely to approach the butyl acetate food lawn than well-fed controls.
source: Indeed, when we tested fasted animals undergoing osmotic stress, they were no more likely to approach the butyl acetate food lawn than well-fed controls (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data for animals fasted under osmotic stress, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: AWA displays notable calcium peaks as animals navigate toward a food lawn.
source: Across conditions, AWA displayed notable calcium peaks as animals navigated toward the food lawn (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by freely moving calcium imaging data showing AWA GCaMP peaks during food approach, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AWA calcium responses to food mostly occurred when animals were in close proximity to the food lawn and when they were moving up the odor gradient toward the food.
source: These responses mostly occurred when animals were in close proximity to the food lawn and when they were moving up the odor gradient toward the food.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of freely moving calcium imaging data showing spatial and temporal patterns of AWA responses.

claim: The amplitudes of AWA calcium peaks in response to food were significantly increased in fasted animals compared to fed animals.
source: The amplitudes and durations of these peaks were significantly increased in fasted animals compared to fed animals (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of AWA GCaMP peak amplitudes in freely moving animals, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The durations of AWA calcium peaks in response to food were significantly increased in fasted animals compared to fed animals.
source: The amplitudes and durations of these peaks were significantly increased in fasted animals compared to fed animals (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of AWA GCaMP peak durations in freely moving animals, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The fasting-induced increase in AWA food responses was attenuated by exposing animals to mild osmotic stress during fasting.
source: The fasting-induced increase in AWA food responses was attenuated by exposing animals to mild osmotic stress during fasting (Figure 3C and D), matching the above results that this stressor suppresses the fasting-induced increase in str-44 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by freely moving calcium imaging data showing reduced AWA responses in animals fasted under osmotic stress, as shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Fed animals overexpressing str-44 and srd-28 in AWA showed a marked decrease in exploration on food, mimicking the behavior of fasted wild-type animals.
source: Indeed, we observed that overexpressing str-44 and srd-28 in AWA led to a marked decrease in exploration in the fed state, mimicking the behavior of fasted wild-type animals (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by on-food exploration assay data showing reduced movement in fed animals overexpressing str-44 and srd-28, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The effect of str-44 and srd-28 overexpression on movement was only observed in the presence of bacterial food.
source: This effect on movement was only observed in the presence of bacterial food as the same overexpression strain displayed wild-type speed in the absence of food (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by locomotion assay data showing normal speed off food in animals overexpressing str-44 and srd-28, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Well-fed tax-4 mutants exhibited a striking increase in str-44 expression compared to wild-type controls, with expression levels even greater than wild-type fasted animals.
source: Well-fed tax-4 mutants exhibited a striking increase in str-44 expression compared to wild-type controls, with expression levels even greater than wild-type fasted animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in tax-4 mutants, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Well-fed tax-4 mutants exhibited increased attraction to butyl acetate.
source: Correspondingly, well-fed tax-4 mutants exhibited increased attraction to the STR-44-sensed odor butyl acetate (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data for tax-4 mutants, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: tax-4 animals displayed normal feeding rates.
source: A potential concern is that an increase in str-44 expression may occur if a mutation reduces food intake; however, we found that tax-4 animals displayed normal feeding rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows normal feeding rates for tax-4 and all other mutants/transgenics with elevated str-44 expression in fed animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharyngeal pumping rate measurements, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The elevated str-44 expression in tax-4 mutants could be rescued by expressing the tax-4 cDNA under its own promoter.
source: This phenotype could be rescued by expressing the tax-4 cDNA under its own promoter (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in tax-4 mutants with tax-4 rescue construct, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: tax-4 mutants have elevated expression of the AWA chemoreceptor srd-28.
source: In addition, we found that tax-4 mutants also have elevated expression of another AWA chemoreceptor, srd-28 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of srd-28::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in tax-4 mutants, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals.
source: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB, BAG, ASI, AQR/PQR/URX, or ASK via a histamine-gated chloride channel (HisCl) (Pokala et al., 2014) led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals, whereas ASJ silencing had no effect (Figure 4B; feeding controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with AWB silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4B, and cites the HisCl method (Pokala et al., 2014).

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of BAG led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals.
source: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB, BAG, ASI, AQR/PQR/URX, or ASK via a histamine-gated chloride channel (HisCl) (Pokala et al., 2014) led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals, whereas ASJ silencing had no effect (Figure 4B; feeding controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with BAG silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4B, and cites the HisCl method (Pokala et al., 2014).

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of ASI led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals.
source: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB, BAG, ASI, AQR/PQR/URX, or ASK via a histamine-gated chloride channel (HisCl) (Pokala et al., 2014) led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals, whereas ASJ silencing had no effect (Figure 4B; feeding controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with ASI silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4B, and cites the HisCl method (Pokala et al., 2014).

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of AQR/PQR/URX led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals.
source: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB, BAG, ASI, AQR/PQR/URX, or ASK via a histamine-gated chloride channel (HisCl) (Pokala et al., 2014) led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals, whereas ASJ silencing had no effect (Figure 4B; feeding controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with AQR/PQR/URX silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4B, and cites the HisCl method (Pokala et al., 2014).

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of ASK led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals.
source: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB, BAG, ASI, AQR/PQR/URX, or ASK via a histamine-gated chloride channel (HisCl) (Pokala et al., 2014) led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals, whereas ASJ silencing had no effect (Figure 4B; feeding controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with ASK silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4B, and cites the HisCl method (Pokala et al., 2014).

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of ASJ had no effect on str-44 expression in well-fed animals.
source: Chemogenetic silencing of AWB, BAG, ASI, AQR/PQR/URX, or ASK via a histamine-gated chloride channel (HisCl) (Pokala et al., 2014) led to a significant increase in str-44 expression in well-fed animals, whereas ASJ silencing had no effect (Figure 4B; feeding controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with ASJ silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4B, and cites the HisCl method (Pokala et al., 2014).

claim: Loss of the daf-2 insulin receptor caused a strong de-repression of str-44.
source: Loss of the daf-2 insulin receptor also caused a strong de-repression of str-44 and a corresponding increase in butyl acetate attraction (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in daf-2 mutants, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of the daf-2 insulin receptor caused a corresponding increase in butyl acetate attraction.
source: Loss of the daf-2 insulin receptor also caused a strong de-repression of str-44 and a corresponding increase in butyl acetate attraction (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by food choice assay data for daf-2 mutants, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: daf-16 mutants showed nearly abolished str-44 expression.
source: Conversely, daf-16 mutants showed nearly abolished str-44 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in daf-16 mutants, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of the daf-2 cDNA specifically in AWA rescued str-44 expression to wild-type levels in daf-2 mutants.
source: Expression of the daf-2 cDNA specifically in AWA rescued str-44 expression to wild-type levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in daf-2 mutants with AWA-specific daf-2 rescue, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of the daf-16a cDNA specifically in AWA rescued str-44 expression in daf-16 mutants, albeit not completely.
source: Expression of the daf-16a cDNA specifically in AWA rescued str-44 expression, albeit not completely; expression of this cDNA in all tissues yielded the same result, suggesting that additional isoforms of daf-16 are required (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in daf-16 mutants with AWA-specific daf-16a rescue, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: daf-2 and daf-16 mutants respectively increase and decrease srd-28 expression in AWA.
source: Finally, we determined that daf-2 and daf-16 mutants respectively increase and decrease srd-28 expression in AWA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of srd-28::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in daf-2 and daf-16 mutants, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: AWA-specific expression of Gao/goa-1(gf) drove a robust increase in str-44 expression.
source: AWA-specific expression of Gao/goa-1(gf) or acy-1(gf), a key Gas/gsa-1 effector, drove a robust increase in str-44 expression, whereas expression of Gaq/egl-30(gf) had only a mild effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals expressing goa-1(gf) in AWA, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AWA-specific expression of acy-1(gf) drove a robust increase in str-44 expression.
source: AWA-specific expression of Gao/goa-1(gf) or acy-1(gf), a key Gas/gsa-1 effector, drove a robust increase in str-44 expression, whereas expression of Gaq/egl-30(gf) had only a mild effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals expressing acy-1(gf) in AWA, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AWA-specific expression of Gaq/egl-30(gf) had only a mild effect on str-44 expression.
source: AWA-specific expression of Gao/goa-1(gf) or acy-1(gf), a key Gas/gsa-1 effector, drove a robust increase in str-44 expression, whereas expression of Gaq/egl-30(gf) had only a mild effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals expressing egl-30(gf) in AWA, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Synaptic silencing of AIA led to a significant decrease in str-44 expression in fasted animals.
source: Synaptic silencing of AIA led to a significant decrease in str-44 expression in fasted animals, whereas synaptic silencing of AIY had no effect (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with AIA synaptically silenced by TeTx, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Synaptic silencing of AIY had no effect on str-44 expression.
source: Synaptic silencing of AIA led to a significant decrease in str-44 expression in fasted animals, whereas synaptic silencing of AIY had no effect (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with AIY synaptically silenced by TeTx, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Direct chemogenetic silencing of AWA inhibited str-44 expression.
source: In addition, direct chemogenetic silencing of AWA also inhibited str-44 expression, suggesting that modulating AWA activity itself can influence str-44 expression (Figure 4E; histamine controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with AWA silenced by HisCl, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Inhibition of synaptic release from AWA had no effect on str-44 expression.
source: Inhibition of synaptic release from AWA had no effect on str-44 expression, suggesting that AWA activity autonomously controls AWA chemoreceptor levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements of str-44::T2A-mNeonGreen reporter in animals with AWA synaptically silenced by TeTx, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: cat-1/VMAT mutants displayed normal str-44 expression in fed and fasted states.

claim: Loss of rict-1/Rictor led to a robust increase in str-44 expression in fed and fasted animals.

claim: Loss of rict-1/Rictor increased butyl acetate attraction.

claim: Food deprivation leads to exaggerated dwelling upon encountering food in C. elegans.

claim: The effects of hunger in C. elegans are mediated by amines and insulin signaling.
